title: KV Cache Offload & Host Memory Paging — Design Draft
content:
Purpose
This draft explores designs for KV cache offload and CPU/host-memory paging for the serving runtime. Goal is to reduce GPU memory pressure for long-context/large-concurrency workloads while keeping latency regressions within SLOs. We sketch options (PCIe/NVMe offload, UMA/unified-memory host paging), threshold heuristics, eviction and prefetch policies, and integration points with kernel selection and scheduler.

Background and motivation
- High token-length workloads and many concurrent inferences drive KV cache growth (KV size ~ batch * seq_len * hidden * 2 * sizeof(float)).
- GPUs have limited HBM; serving multiple models/versions and supporting Dedicated nodes means we must avoid OOMs while keeping p99 latency low.
- Existing approaches: keep full KV in GPU (fastest), evict entire sequences (accuracy loss on long-range attention), or fall back to smaller model variants (functional but costly).
- Offloading cold KV pages to host/PCIe or NVMe can increase effective cache capacity but introduces latency/cost tradeoffs.

Design goals
- Primary: prevent OOMs and reduce scheduling backpressure under high memory pressure with minimal p99 latency impact.
- Secondary: incremental deployability (soft offload with feature flags), deterministic behavior under failures, observable metrics for offload/paging activity and quality impact.
- Constraints: must work across Hosted/Dedicated/Private; on Private some hardware (NVMe, PCIe topology) varies. Must support both UMA (e.g., AMD Infinity) and discrete GPU + host memory setups.

Key design dimensions
1) Offload medium
- Host DRAM over PCIe (peer-to-host): low latency (~µs-100s µs depending on PCIe gen and topology) but consumes system RAM.
- NVMe (local SSD) via DMA/async IO: higher latency (ms tail), durable, useful for very cold ranges or ephemeral spill; good for multi-tenant eviction to cheaper storage tier.
- GPU Direct Storage or GPUDirect RDMA: for specialized systems, avoids host CPU copies; treat as optimization path.

2) Memory model and placement
- UMA-capable platforms: unified virtual address space allows on-demand paging into host memory with hardware-assisted migration. For UMA we rely on OS/hypervisor support (e.g., AMD/ROCm MIG/UMA semantics). Behavior: mark KV pages as migratable and let kernel/hw migrate on access.
- Discrete GPU (CUDA/HIP): maintain explicit device-side KV cache with a host-side backing store and manual DMA transfers.

3) Thresholds and admission policies
- Global HBM watermark levels: soft_limit, hard_limit. soft_limit triggers proactive offload and throttling; hard_limit triggers eviction/fallback.
- Per-model and per-client budgets: allow pinning critical clients to GPU-resident KV and spill best-effort traffic.
- Eviction candidates: least-recently-used (LRU) at segment granularity (e.g., KV blocks per token-chunk), frequency-aware policies for conversational sessions. Prefer evicting cold prefixes first.

4) Eviction & Prefetching
- Eviction unit: block-size aligned to KV slab (configurable, default 4–16KB logical slabs corresponding to groups of KV vectors).
- Prefetch heuristics: on sequence continuation prediction (session sees new tokens), prefetch next N slabs asynchronously if latency headroom exists.
- Async page-in prioritized by request-criticality (foreground vs background). High-priority requests can trigger synchronous pull if within p50 budget.

5) Scheduling and kernel interaction
- Scheduler integrates offload awareness: request admission uses current HBM utilization and offload bandwidth availability to accept/decline new requests or route to lower-memory variants.
- Kernels must expose memory access hints: kernels reading KV should annotate access patterns so scheduler/paging manager can prefetch hot slabs or throttle streaming workloads.
- Continuous batching: batch composition should consider KV residency—group requests with GPU-resident KV to maximize throughput. If a batch includes both resident and non-resident KV, scheduler can choose to split.

6) Consistency and correctness
- KV pages are immutable for the life of a request except for append of new entries; this simplifies eviction (no writeback needed).
- For attention caches (KV for autoregressive decoding) the only mutation is append; offload policy must ensure appended pages are promoted as needed.

7) Observability and SLOs
- Metrics: hbm_utilization_pct, host_kv_pages, nvme_spill_io_rate, average_offload_latency, page_fault_rate, prefetch_hit_rate, evictions_per_min, requests_routed_to_small_variant.
- Tracing: tag requests with offload events and measure per-request added latency due to page-in.
- Alerts: sustained paging above threshold, IO queue saturation, or prefetch miss storms.

Implementation options (ranked by expected complexity vs benefit)
A) Host DRAM spill (manual DMA) — recommended default
- Keep primary KV in GPU; when HBM >= soft_limit, pick cold slabs and async copy to pinned host buffers via CUDA pinned memory or equivalent.
- On access, async page-in; if access happens during critical path and pending page-in latency exceeds threshold, scheduler can either block short time or fall back to smaller model or route to different node.
Pros: relatively low latency vs NVMe, simple semantics. Cons: uses host RAM and PCIe bandwidth.

B) UMA/hardware-assisted paging — opportunistic for UMA nodes
- When available, rely on OS/hw to migrate pages. We expose madvise/mmap-like layers and mark memory as migratable with coarse hints.
Pros: minimal changes in runtime, potentially low overhead. Cons: unpredictable latency and platform-dependent behavior; hard to guarantee SLOs.

C) NVMe spill (cold tier)
- Evict very cold KV to local NVMe using async IO and maintain index in host memory. Only used for long-idle sessions or large-scale archival spill.
Pros: cheap capacity, persistent across restarts. Cons: ms tail; use only for very cold data.

Heuristics and thresholds (initial proposal)
- soft_limit = 75% HBM usage: begin proactive offload and prefetch rate-limiting.
- hard_limit = 92% HBM usage: disallow accepting new high-memory requests; aggressive eviction to hit target 70%.
- PCIe latency budget per page-in: target p95 page-in < 200 µs for host DRAM spill. If p95 > target, increase prefetch aggressiveness or reject requests.
- Prefetch window: prefetch up to next 2 slabs for active sessions; reduce for heavy multi-tenant situations.
- Per-session pinned quota default 0.5% HBM but configurable for enterprise customers.

Failure modes and fallback policies
- PCIe bandwidth saturation: detect and throttle offload/prefetch rates; expose backpressure to scheduler to route traffic.
- Host OOM due to excessive spills: enforce global host-spill budget and fall back to reject/route requests or NVMe spill.
- NVMe failures: maintain retry/backoff and mark device unhealthy.

Integration with rollout and config
- Feature flags: enable_offload, offload_mode = (host|nvme|uma|auto), soft_limit, hard_limit, slab_size.
- Canary plan: staged rollout on Dedicated nodes; collect offload metrics and p99 latency regression per-model before broader rollout.

Benchmarks to run
- Microbench: single-request page-in latency for various slab sizes and PCIe generations.
- Throughput test: many concurrent sessions with long contexts to measure throughput p50/p95 with and without offload.
- Mixed workload: mix of short low-memory and long high-memory sessions to validate scheduler routing and prefetch policies.
- Failure injection: saturate PCIe bandwidth and simulate host OOM.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Granularity: slab vs token-level vectors. Smaller slabs increase metadata overhead and IO ops; larger slabs waste memory.
- Prefetch accuracy vs wasted bandwidth: how aggressive should prefetch be for conversational flows? Could ML-based predictors help? (TODO evaluate simple Markov predictor.)
- What guarantees can UMA provide across cloud providers? Need test matrix for representative hardware.

Next steps / TODOs
- Spike: implement host DRAM offload prototype in rust runtime (async copy + slab index) and measure p95 page-in on PCIe Gen3 vs Gen4.
- Evaluate UMA behavior on AMD testbeds and draft platform-specific guidelines.
- Build observability dashboards for offload metrics and add tracing hooks to request lifecycle.
- Write scheduler integration proposal (separate PRD) to wire offload signals into admission control.

Appendix: rough API sketches (informal)
- OffloadManager.offload_slab(model_id, slab_id) -> async token (string) for tracking
- OffloadManager.prefetch_slabs(session_id, [slab_ids], priority)
- Scheduler.query_offload_budget(node_id) -> {hbm_pct, host_spill_used}
- Kernel hinting: Kernel.launch(..., kv_access_hints=Bitmap)

Notes to reviewers
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: prefer host-DRAM offload first, UMA opportunistic, NVMe for cold-tier only.
- Looking for feedback on thresholds, slab size defaults, and how to expose per-customer pinned quotas in Dedicated/Private.
- cc: eng-serving-runtime, infra, release-eng for rollout constraints.
notes: This document is a design draft intended for internal review.
